fields.Trigger: First cost incurred on approved capex project
fields.Volume: ~30–50 active CIP accounts at any time (one per active capex project, per the PA-40.1 ~30–50-project register)

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-count of "account structure in GL" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-review of "review per W1705" (replaces manual Step 2).
Controls: - CTL-363 (ensure controlled execution — Construction-in-Progress & Asset Turnover (PA-40.3).)
- operational: Project Accountant review and approval gate; periodic reconciliation against source documents
Pain Points / Risks: - **Aging-CIP risk**: projects complete but costs linger in CIP, overstating PP&E and dodging depreciation; mitigated by monthly roll-forward with turnover follow-up (step 2)
- **Impairment-blindness risk**: stalled projects carried at cost despite no future benefit; mitigated by PAS 36 impairment assessment (step 4)
System Touchpoints: - CIP account structure — one GL CIP account per active project (step 1)
- Monthly CIP management — accumulation without depreciation, roll-forward (step 2)
- Balance-sheet presentation within PP&E (step 3)
- Impairment assessment for stalled/abandoned projects per PAS 36 (step 4)
Time Estimate: CIP account structure maintained per project; monthly CIP management within the close ≈ 4–8 hours/month ≈ 48–96 hours/year across ~10–20 active accounts; balance-sheet presentation at reporting dates; impairment assessment on stall/abandonment triggers per W1700.

steps.activity: CIP account structure in GL: (a) one CIP account per active capex project (e.g., CIP-BRD-001 Mindanao Store, CIP-IT-ERP-Upgrade), (b) sub-accounts by cost category: materials, labor, services, equipment, professional fees, capitalized interest, (c) entity-specific: each entity's CIP tracked separately, (d) group-level CIP visible for consolidation

Monthly CIP management: (a) all project costs accumulated in CIP (not depreciated — CIP assets are not yet in use), (b) monthly review per W1705 (CIP reconciliation), (c) CIP aging report: flag projects in CIP > 12 months (risk of stalled or abandoned projects), (d) CIP balance should increase as project progresses and decrease to zero when asset is turned over

CIP balance sheet presentation: (a) CIP classified as non-current asset (part of Property, Plant & Equipment) in balance sheet, (b) separate line item or combined with fixed assets (materiality-dependent), (c) CIP balance = total costs incurred but not yet capitalized as completed assets
Impairment of CIP: if project is stalled or abandoned, CIP must be assessed for impairment per PAS 36 (same as W1700 for completed assets); abandoned projects written off per W2750

fields.Frequency: ~10–15 store completions/year + ~20–35 other capex project completions (remodels, DC, IT, equipment)
fields.Participants: Project Manager, COO, Store Manager (for new stores), Project Accountant, Fixed Asset Accountant
fields.Trigger: Project reaches practical completion (asset ready for intended use)

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-inspect of "Project Manager confirms practical completion" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-document of "documented with agreed resolution timeline" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-review of "reviews all CIP costs for completeness and accuracy" (replaces manual Step 3).
Controls: - CTL-363 (ensure controlled execution — Construction-in-Progress & Asset Turnover (PA-40.3).)
- operational: COO (construction) / CIO (IT) / Department Head (other) review and approval gate
Pain Points / Risks: - **Premature-turnover risk**: asset declared complete while materially unfinished, starting depreciation early; mitigated by practical-completion criteria (step 1)
- **Cost-completeness risk**: late invoices arrive after CIP is cleared; mitigated by completeness review plus post-turnover charge controls (step 3)
System Touchpoints: - Practical completion confirmation — work complete, asset ready for use (step 1)
- Completion certificate — PM certifies, COO/CIO accepts, Store Manager receives (step 2)
- Cost completeness review before turnover initiation (step 3)
Time Estimate: 4–6 days elapsed per occurrence (1 day + 1 day + 2–4 days) — at ~10–15 store completions/year + ~20–35 other project completions ≈ 30–50 occurrences/year.

steps.activity: Project Manager confirms practical completion: (a) all construction/installation work complete (punch list items may remain but are not critical to operation), (b) systems tested and operational (IT projects: UAT passed; stores: POS live), (c) safety inspection passed, (d) occupancy permit received (if required), (e) asset is **ready for its intended use** per PFRS — this is the trigger for depreciation start (not the grand opening date)

Completion certificate prepared and signed: (a) Project Manager certifies completion, (b) COO or CIO accepts, (c) Store Manager (for new stores) confirms operational readiness, (d) punch list items documented with agreed resolution timeline

Project Accountant initiates CIP-to-asset turnover per W1829: (a) reviews all CIP costs for completeness and accuracy, (b) ensures all invoices received and allocated, (c) accrues any known but uninvoiced costs, (d) transfers CIP balance to completed fixed assets

fields.Participants: Fixed Asset Accountant, Project Accountant, Accounting Manager
fields.Volume: 1 conversion per completed project (may result in multiple fixed assets)

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-count of "Accountant decomposes project cost into component assets per W1694" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-record of "records created with component structures" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-post of "Journal entries posted" (replaces manual Step 3).
Controls: - CTL-363 (ensure controlled execution — Construction-in-Progress & Asset Turnover (PA-40.3).)
- operational: standard operating procedures; system-enforced validation rules
Pain Points / Risks: - **Componentization error**: everything depreciated on a single life, misstating expense timing; mitigated by component decomposition per W1694 (step 1)
- **Conversion-imbalance risk**: assets created ≠ CIP cleared; mitigated by balance verification with unexplained-difference investigation (step 4)
System Touchpoints: - Component decomposition per W1694 — building, fixtures, POS, HVAC with separate lives (step 1)
- CIP-to-asset conversion processing — CIP cleared, asset records created (step 2)
- Journal entries and depreciation-start setup (step 3)
- Verification — total assets = CIP balance before conversion (step 4)
Time Estimate: 1 day elapsed per occurrence (1 day); cadence-carried steps as authored (1–2 days/project) — at ~30–50 conversions/year ≈ 30–50 occurrences/year.

steps.activity: Fixed Asset Accountant decomposes project cost into component assets per W1694: (a) **new store example** (total cost PHP 50M): (i) leasehold improvements: PHP 20M (depreciate over lease term 10–15 years), (ii) HVAC system: PHP 5M (10–15 years), (iii) electrical installation: PHP 4M (15–20 years), (iv) plumbing: PHP 3M (15–20 years), (v) racking/shelving: PHP 5M (10 years), (vi) POS system (3 terminals): PHP 1.5M (5 years), (vii) signage: PHP 2M (7–10 years), (viii) generator: PHP 1.5M (7 years), (ix) CCTV system: PHP 1M (5 years), (x) initial inventory: PHP 5M (not fixed asset — transferred to inventory), (xi) pre-opening expenses (training, marketing): PHP 2M (not fixed asset — expensed), (xii) contingency unused: returned to capex pool

System processes CIP-to-asset conversion: (a) CIP account debited to zero, (b) new fixed asset records created with component structures, (c) each component assigned useful life and depreciation method per W1691, (d) depreciation begins from the **ready-for-use date** (completion certificate date, not grand opening date), (e) pre-opening and non-capitalizable costs reclassified from CIP to expense

Journal entries posted: (a) debit: fixed asset accounts (gross) per component, (b) credit: CIP account (cleared to zero), (c) debit: pre-opening expense (for non-capitalized costs), (d) debit: inventory (for initial stock), (e) credit: CIP (for above reclassifications)

Fixed Asset Accountant verifies new asset records: (a) total asset value = CIP balance before conversion (no unexplained difference), (b) depreciation start date correct, (c) useful life per component is appropriate, (d) asset tags ordered per W1692

fields.Frequency: ~30–50 post-implementation reviews/year (one per completed project, per W1828)
fields.Participants: FP&A, Project Sponsor, Department Head, CFO

workflows.name: Post-Implementation Review & Actual vs. Projected ROI Analysis

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-calculate of "recalculate with actual cash flows" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-measure of "For non-revenue projects" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-review of "FP&A prepares post-implementation review report" (replaces manual Step 3).
Controls: - CTL-363 (ensure controlled execution — Construction-in-Progress & Asset Turnover (PA-40.3).)
- operational: FP&A review and approval gate
Pain Points / Risks: - **No-lookback risk**: projects approved, delivered, and never judged against promises; mitigated by the mandatory 12-month review (step 1)
- **Systematic-optimism risk**: the same estimation bias repeats every year; mitigated by annual bias compilation feeding W2752 calibration (step 4)
System Touchpoints: - Actual vs. business-case comparison — cost, revenue, schedule at 12 months (step 1)
- Non-revenue project benefit measurement — savings and operational improvements (step 2)
- Post-implementation review report with learnings (step 3)
- Annual cross-project compilation identifying estimation biases (step 4)
Time Estimate: 1 day elapsed per occurrence (1 day); cadence-carried steps as authored (1–2 days/project, 1 day/project, 1 day/year) — at ~30–50 post-implementation reviews/year (per the Frequency) ≈ 30–50 occurrences/year.

steps.activity: FP&A compares actual project outcomes to original business case: (a) **cost**: actual total cost vs. approved budget (typically actual is 5–15% over budget for construction projects), (b) **timeline**: actual completion date vs. planned (typically 1–3 months delayed), (c) **revenue**: for new stores — actual Year 1 revenue vs. projected revenue per W1652, (d) **profitability**: store EBITDA margin vs. projected, (e) **payback**: actual payback trajectory vs. projected payback period, (f) **IRR/NPV**: recalculate with actual cash flows

For non-revenue projects (IT, equipment replacement): (a) cost savings achieved vs. projected, (b) operational improvements measured vs. baseline, (c) user satisfaction survey, (d) compliance achieved (if regulatory project)

FP&A prepares post-implementation review report: (a) summary of actual vs. projected, (b) key learnings (what went well, what didn't), (c) calibration: how accurate were original projections? (d) recommendations for future similar projects, (e) presented to steering committee or CFO

Annual: FP&A compiles post-implementation results across all completed projects; identifies systematic biases in project estimation (e.g., consistently overestimating revenue, underestimating costs); adjusts estimation methodology for future business cases

fields.Frequency: ~5–10 partial turnovers/year (primarily multi-store builds, DC expansions)
fields.Participants: Fixed Asset Accountant, Project Manager, Accounting Manager
fields.Trigger: Part of a large project is ready for use before the entire project is complete

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-log of "Fixed Asset Accountant allocates CIP costs between completed and" (replaces manual Step 2).
Controls: - operational: standard operating procedures; system-enforced validation rules
Pain Points / Risks: - **Arbitrary-split risk**: the completed/in-progress cost split is guesswork, misstating both depreciation and remaining CIP; mitigated by specific-cost identification with documented allocation (step 2)
- **Depreciation-start error**: wings in use but not depreciated; mitigated by depreciation commencing on partial turnover (step 3)
System Touchpoints: - Partial turnover scenarios — DC wings, multi-store programs (step 1)
- CIP cost allocation between completed and in-progress portions (step 2)
- Partial conversion processing with depreciation starting on the completed portion (step 3)
Time Estimate: ~1–2 days per partial turnover (CIP cost allocation between completed and in-progress portions + system transfer to fixed assets) × ~5–10 partial turnovers/year ≈ 5–20 days/year.

steps.activity: Scenarios requiring partial turnover: (a) DC expansion: new wing operational while second wing still under construction, (b) multi-store build: first 3 stores of a 5-store batch open before remaining 2, (c) IT rollout: phase 1 modules live while phase 2 still in development

Fixed Asset Accountant allocates CIP costs between completed and in-progress portions: (a) completed portion: identify specific costs attributable to the ready-for-use portion, (b) in-progress portion: remaining costs stay in CIP, (c) apportionment methodology: direct identification where possible; proportional allocation for shared costs (e.g., project management, permits)

System processes partial turnover: (a) completed portion transferred from CIP to fixed assets, (b) depreciation begins on completed portion, (c) remaining CIP continues to accumulate costs until next phase completes, (d) subsequent turnovers processed same way until project fully complete

fields.Frequency: ~1–3 abandoned projects/year (low frequency but high impact)
fields.Participants: CFO, FP&A, Project Manager, CEO, Board
fields.Trigger: Decision to abandon or indefinitely suspend a capex project

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-issue of "issues discovered during construction" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-count of "CFO and FP&A assess financial impact" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-record of "recorded as receivable" (replaces manual Step 4).
Controls: - CTL-363 (ensure controlled execution — Construction-in-Progress & Asset Turnover (PA-40.3).)
- operational: CFO review and approval gate
Pain Points / Risks: - **Zombie-project risk**: abandoned projects carried indefinitely in CIP; mitigated by write-off approval tiers forcing recognition (steps 3–4)
- **Recovery-overstatement risk**: salvage values assumed but never realized; mitigated by recoverables recorded separately from the write-off (step 4)
System Touchpoints: - Abandonment triggers — site issues, market shifts (step 1)
- Financial impact assessment — CIP incurred, salvage/recovery potential (step 2)
- Tiered write-off approval — CFO < PHP 5M; CEO PHP 5–50M; Board > PHP 50M (step 3)
- Write-off processing with recoveries recorded separately (step 4)
Time Estimate: 2.3–4 weeks elapsed per occurrence (1–2 weeks + 1–5 days + 1–2 days + 1 week); cadence-carried steps as authored (Event-driven) — at ~1–3 abandoned projects/year (low frequency but high impact) ≈ 1–3 occurrences/year.

steps.activity: Triggers for project abandonment: (a) site issues discovered during construction (soil, legal, environmental), (b) market conditions change (trade area no longer viable — competitor opens nearby, economic downturn), (c) regulatory block (permit denied, zoning change), (d) strategic pivot (company changes expansion plan), (e) contractor failure (contractor abandons project)

CFO and FP&A assess financial impact: (a) total CIP costs incurred to date, (b) recovery potential: (i) materials salvageable and reusable (transfer to other projects), (ii) equipment already purchased (sell, return to vendor, or redeploy), (iii) contractor claims and counterclaims, (iv) insurance recovery (if applicable), (c) net write-off amount = CIP costs − recoveries
Write-off approval: (a) < PHP 5M: CFO approval, (b) PHP 5–50M: CEO approval, (c) > PHP 50M: Board approval, (d) write-off recognized as non-current asset disposal loss (not inventory write-off)

Write-off processing: (a) CIP balance written off to P&L (debit: project abandonment loss, credit: CIP), (b) recoverable amounts recorded as receivable, (c) when recovery received: credit to project abandonment loss (partial offset), (d) Board notified at next meeting regardless of amount
Lessons learned documented per W2751; preventive measures implemented to reduce future abandonment risk

fields.Participants: Project Manager, Project Accountant, COO, FP&A
fields.Trigger: Project completed and asset turned over (W1828–1829) or abandoned (W2750)

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-review of "review scheduled per W2748" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-record of "records" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-document of "documentation retained for asset useful life + 10 years" (replaces manual Step 3).
Controls: - CTL-363 (ensure controlled execution — Construction-in-Progress & Asset Turnover (PA-40.3).)
- operational: Project Manager review and approval gate
Pain Points / Risks: - **Open-tail risk**: project closed with open POs or unpaid claims surfacing later; mitigated by the closeout checklist (step 1)
- **Post-close-charge risk**: costs keep landing on a completed project; mitigated by the system block on closed projects (step 4)
System Touchpoints: - Closeout checklist — costs complete, POs closed, vendor claims settled (step 1)
- Documentation archive — full project file (step 2)
- Retention for asset life + 10 years for tax/audit (step 3)
- System status "Closed" blocking further charges (step 4)
Time Estimate: 2.1–3.1 weeks elapsed per occurrence (1–2 weeks + 1 week + 1 day) — at ~30–50 closeouts/year ≈ 30–50 occurrences/year.

steps.activity: Project closeout checklist: (a) all costs received and allocated to project, (b) all POs closed (no open commitments), (c) all vendor invoices received and paid (including retention release if applicable), (d) CIP account cleared (zero balance after turnover), (e) fixed assets registered per W1690, (f) asset tags applied per W1692, (g) project completion certificate signed, (h) post-implementation review scheduled per W2748

Documentation archive: (a) original capex request and business case, (b) financial evaluation and approval documentation, (c) all vendor contracts and POs, (d) contractor progress billings and payment records, (e) change orders with approvals, (f) completion certificate and turnover documentation, (g) warranty certificates from contractors and equipment vendors, (h) as-built drawings (for construction projects), (i) post-implementation review, (j) budget vs. actual final report

Archive retention: (a) project documentation retained for asset useful life + 10 years (for tax and audit purposes), (b) stored in document management system (electronic) and physical archive (for signed originals), (c) indexed by project number for retrieval
System project status changed to "Closed"; no further costs can be charged to the project

fields.Participants: CFO, FP&A, VP Store Operations, COO, CIO, CEO

workflows.name: Annual Capex Portfolio Review & Process Improvement

Automation Opportunity: - System auto-review of "FP&A prepares annual capex portfolio review" (replaces manual Step 1).
- System auto-issue of "issues cause overruns?" (replaces manual Step 2).
- System auto-log of "Process improvements identified and implemented" (replaces manual Step 3).
Controls: - CTL-363 (ensure controlled execution — Construction-in-Progress & Asset Turnover (PA-40.3).)
- operational: CFO review and approval gate
Pain Points / Risks: - **Repeat-overspend risk**: chronic overruns recur without methodology correction; mitigated by estimation calibration from actuals (step 3)
- **Guideline-decay risk**: improved procedures documented but never adopted; mitigated by distribution with training as a closing step (step 4)
System Touchpoints: - Annual portfolio review — spend vs. budget by category, returns by project type (steps 1–2)
- Process improvements — estimation calibration, approval thresholds (step 3)
- Updated guidelines distributed with stakeholder training (step 4)
Time Estimate: 2 hours per occurrence (per-step effort 2 hours); elapsed timeline 1 week + 1–2 weeks + 1 week — at Annual ≈ 1 occurrence/year ≈ 2 hours/year.

steps.activity: FP&A prepares annual capex portfolio review: (a) total capex spent vs. budget (by category: new stores, renovations, DC, IT, equipment), (b) project delivery performance: % on time, % on budget, % achieving projected ROI, (c) cost estimation accuracy: average budget variance per project type, (d) timeline estimation accuracy: average schedule variance, (e) post-implementation ROI results: actual vs. projected across completed projects, (f) abandoned project cost and reasons, (g) capital productivity: revenue growth ÷ capex invested

CFO and C-Suite review capex portfolio performance: (a) which project types deliver best returns (new stores vs. renovations vs. IT)? (b) what systemic issues cause overruns? (c) what estimation biases need correction? (d) is capex spend aligned with strategic priorities?

Process improvements identified and implemented: (a) estimation methodology: adjust cost escalation factors based on actual construction inflation, (b) approval process: streamline for repeatable project types (new stores have standardized approval), (c) contractor management: update contractor qualification criteria based on performance, (d) system enhancements: automate CIP-to-asset conversion, improve cost tracking granularity per W1810
Updated capex process guidelines distributed to all project stakeholders; training provided for new procedures
